name: Glass skin routine

lead: Glass skin is a look of smooth, even, luminous skin that appears almost translucent, popularised through Korean skincare and social media. People pursue it for a dewy, pore-minimal complexion.

The routine layers products: oil and water cleansers, gentle exfoliation, hydrating essences or ampoules, moisturiser and sunscreen. The visual effect is attributed to hydration, even texture and reduced inflammation. On looksmax.org users discuss it as both a goal and a routine and debate how much depends on genetics versus diet and skincare. No published study evaluates the glass skin routine itself.

paras: Posters describe double cleansing, gentle chemical exfoliation (BHA/AHA) about once a week, hydrating essences or ampoules, moisturiser and daily sunscreen, plus attention to diet and hydration. People build it up step by step and judge results over weeks as texture and hydration improve.

Overuse of exfoliating acids is a commonly discussed irritation risk, which some posters themselves caution against. Forum posts also mix routine advice with dietary claims and talk of prescription acne drugs, which are separate from the routine itself.

social.title: Help me get glass skin in my forties!

angle.text: Glass skin is a K-beauty goal of smooth, translucent, dewy skin, pursued with a layered routine of cleansing, exfoliating and hydrating steps. Better hydration and even texture give the poreless, glowing look. It is as much an aesthetic ideal as a defined protocol, and no studies of the routine as a whole exist.

lead: Glass skin is a skincare goal from Korean beauty culture: skin that looks smooth, even, pore-minimal and faintly translucent, with a dewy sheen. People pursue it with a layered routine of cleansing, gentle exfoliation, hydrating essences or ampoules, moisturiser and daily sunscreen, aiming for a clearer, more luminous complexion that reads as healthy and youthful in person and in photos.[1]

Wikipedia describes the look as favoured in South Korea and achieved less through foundation than through a long skincare routine, averaging around ten steps, that starts with a double cleanse and moves through sheet masks, essences, serums and moisturiser to SPF sunscreen by day.[1] The term spread through social media, and on looksmax.org it appears both as a trend and as a routine people try to follow for acne and texture.[2][3]

No clinical study has tested a glass skin routine as a whole. Its individual parts, such as moisturiser, sunscreen, cleansing and exfoliation, are covered in general skin care references, which also note that over-exfoliation can cause irritation and barrier damage.[4]
infobox: Double cleanse, exfoliation, essence, ampoule, moisturiser, sunscreen

paras: Wikipedia's K-beauty article describes a routine that begins with a double cleanse, continues through sheet masks, essences, lotions, serums and rich moisturisers, and ends with SPF sunscreen in the daytime or a thicker sleep cream at night.[1] A representative looksmax.org guide lists an oil-based cleanser, then a water-based cleanser, a BHA or AHA exfoliant about once a week, a moisturising essence, an ampoule, moisturiser and sunscreen, with a food list and advice to drink plenty of water.[2] Another poster describes a simpler acne-focused version: a foaming cleanser, a chemical exfoliant, avoiding physical scrubs while acne is active, plus diet and water changes.[3]

Korean beauty traces its roots to the Three Kingdoms period, with the Goryeo era regarded as a peak, and reached Western markets in 2011 with the BB cream, according to Wikipedia.[1] Asia-Pacific held the largest market share as of 2020, and the Korean Wave of dramas and music has been credited with driving sales.[1] Glass skin spread globally through social media as a visual shorthand for the whole routine.

sections.h: Components and general skin care background
paras: General skin care references describe cleansers as removing oil, dirt and makeup with surfactants, with synthetic detergent cleansers milder than traditional alkaline soap.[4] Moisturisers raise skin water content through humectants, occlusives and emollients, and sunscreen shields skin from UV damage that causes sunburn and premature aging.[4]

Chemical exfoliants are described as generally gentler than mechanical scrubs, but excessive exfoliation can cause irritation and barrier damage, and people with inflammatory acne are advised to exfoliate cautiously.[4]

Forum threads on glass skin range from routine guides to before-and-after acne accounts.[2][3] One poster asked whether anyone had reached the look through lifestyle and skincare alone, suggesting people who have it often already had a good genetic base; a reply credited the product centella for the glassy finish.[5] A Lemmy skincare thread shows the same interest outside looksmaxxing, from a woman in her forties asking how to get the glassy look.[6]
No studies found. The routine's individual components, such as sunscreen, retinoids or acne treatment, are studied separately in the dermatology literature but not as a glass skin protocol.

lore.intro: Glass skin is discussed on looksmax.org as both a K-beauty trend and a skincare goal, with threads giving routines and personal before-and-after accounts.[2][3][5]
